articles.body:
Núcleo de Práticas Jurídicas da UFJF está com vagas abertas para atendimento gratuito à população — Foto: Divulgação / UFJF

O Núcleo de Práticas Jurídicas da Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora (UFJF) está com vagas abertas para atendimento gratuito à população . O serviço oferece orientações relacionadas a divórcio, pensão alimentícia, ação de guarda, inventário, entre outras.

A iniciativa busca facilitar o acesso à Justiça para pessoas que precisam de assistência jurídica, mas não têm condições de arcar com os custos do serviço.

Os atendimentos são voltados para duas áreas:

Sucessões , que inclui casos de usucapião, inventário e registros públicos;

Família , com demandas relacionadas a divórcio, união estável, pensão alimentícia, ação de guarda, interdição e curatela.

Para participar, os interessados devem morar em Juiz de Fora e ter renda familiar máxima de até dois salários mínimos (R$ 3.242).

O agendamento deve ser feito de forma presencial, de segunda a sexta-feira, das 8h às 18h, no Núcleo de Práticas Jurídicas, localizado na avenida Presidente Itamar Franco, n° 988, no Centro. É necessário apresentar RG, CPF e comprovantes de residência e renda.

articles.summary: A avaliação de envolvidos nesta história é que a "crise está longe do fim". Há expectativa de que venham a público dados de outras investigações que podem respingar no calendário eleitoral.
articles.body:
Nos bastidores, a avaliação que une personagens de lados opostos é que a crise no Supremo Tribunal Federal está longe do fim - e que as próximas semanas serão tumultuadas. Uma fonte resume o que vem pela frente como um “setembro sangrento”, com expectativas de novos movimentos de diferentes investigações, reação dentro da Corte e efeitos que inevitavelmente vão respingar no calendário eleitoral.

Entre fontes aliadas de André Mendonça , ouvidas pelo blog , o diagnóstico é de que o relatório da Polícia Federal conhecido na segunda-feira (31) seria apenas uma pequena amostra do que ainda pode aparecer. A leitura nesse grupo é de que houve uma tentativa deliberada de criar uma cortina de fumaça em torno do caso Master e de dificultar o avanço das investigações.

Do outro lado dessa disputa, aliados de Alexandre de Moraes , Flávio Dino e integrantes da cúpula da PF enxergam a ofensiva de Mendonça como parte de uma disputa que agora alcança diretamente a própria Polícia Federal, Moraes e o PGR, Paulo Gonet. Na PF, há a avaliação de que Mendonça quer investigar o diretor-geral Andrei Rodrigues — o que elevaria ainda mais a temperatura de uma crise que já deixou de ser apenas uma divergência entre ministros.

E a avaliação de que novos movimentos de investigações sobre casos nas mãos desse grupo também devem vir à tona.

No plenário, sobre o caso específico do relatório do ministro Mendonça, a decisão depende de Edson Fachin. Interlocutores do ministro Mendonça classificam como “protocolar” o envio do caso à presidência do Supremo: a liberação, dizem, ocorreu apenas depois do fim do prazo dado para que fossem prestadas as informações solicitadas por Edson Fachin. Caberá agora ao presidente do STF decidir qual procedimento adotar.

E é justamente aí que começa a próxima batalha: o que, exatamente, poderá ser levado ao plenário e em quais condições.

Montagem com (esq.): Alexandre de Moraes (ministro do STF), Andrei Rodrigues (diretor-geral da PF), Paulo Gonet (PGR) e André Mendonça (ministro do STF) — Foto: Fotos de: Fabio Rodrigues-Pozzebom e José Cruz da Agência Brasil, e Carlos Moura do STF

Na quinta-feira (3), o ministro Edson Fachin determinou que os ministros Alexandre de Moraes, André Mendonça, Paulo Gonet e o diretor-geral da Polícia Federal, Andrei Rodrigues tem cinco dias para prestar esclarecimentos sobre o caso.

Ministros ouvidos pelo blog chamam atenção para um ponto jurídico central: em condições normais, uma investigação é aberta quando há pedido da Procuradoria-Geral da República ou quando a PGR endossa uma iniciativa da Polícia Federal, já que o Ministério Público é o titular da ação penal. A discussão sobre o que efetivamente pode ser submetido ao plenário, portanto, está longe de ser apenas política: passa também pelos limites processuais da atuação do Supremo, da PGR e da PF. Hoje, o que tem é um pedido para anular o material cujo sigilo Mendonça derrubou.

Enquanto isso, o Planalto observa com preocupação outra consequência da guerra: o impacto eleitoral. Há auxiliares de Lula convencidos de que a exposição permanente de Alexandre de Moraes acaba ajudando Flávio Bolsonaro, porque a oposição associa Moraes diretamente ao presidente. Nesse grupo, existe inclusive a avaliação de que esse efeito eleitoral pode ser mais danoso para Lula do que o desgaste provocado pelo caso Lulinha.

É por isso que diferentes lados, mesmo adversários, concordam em um ponto: o que apareceu até agora não encerra a crise. Abre a próxima fase dela.

De um lado, Mendonça e seus aliados sustentam que é preciso impedir interferências e garantir o avanço das apurações do Master. De outro, Moraes, Dino e integrantes da PF enxergam movimentos do ministro como uma ofensiva que pode alcançar a própria direção da corporação, Moraes e a PGR. No meio, Fachin terá de decidir como o Supremo institucionalmente vai processar essa guerra, Zanin tenta manter canais com os diferentes grupos e o governo Lula acompanha uma crise que já começa a fazer as contas de 2026.

A expectativa nos bastidores é de novos relatórios, novos pedidos, novas decisões e novas revelações. A disputa sobre o Master, que começou como uma investigação financeira, virou uma batalha pelo controle da investigação, pelo funcionamento das instituições e, agora, também pela narrativa eleitoral.

articles.title: Capitais registram manifestações contra Alexandre de Moraes, do STF | G1
articles.standfirst: Manifestantes também criticaram o presidente do Congresso, Davi Alcolumbre, por não dar andamento aos pedidos de processos de impeachment do ministro, e protestaram contra o presidente Lula.
articles.summary: Nesta manhã, cinco capitais e o Distrito Federal tiveram protestos organizados por grupos de direita. À tarde estão previstos atos em São Paulo e Recife.
articles.body:
Em paralelo aos desfiles de 7 de Setembro que ocorrem nesta segunda-feira pelo país, ao menos sete capitais brasileiras registraram manifestações com críticas ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes. Os protestos foram organizados por partidos ou movimentos de direita.

Não ocorreram atos contra Moraes em São Paulo e no Rio de Janeiro. No entanto, candidatos à Presidência citaram o ministro ou o Caso Master no Supremo durante participações em atos de campanha. Leia abaixo:

Na capital paulista , Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) criticou Moraes em seu discurso em ato na Avenida Paulista, que teve frases como "Fora Lula, Fora Moraes" vindas de seus apoiadores. Já Romeu Zema (NOVO) estendeu painel em um prédio em que aparecia o boneco de Moraes preso . E Renan Santos (Missão) fez ato no Parque do Ibirapuera e pediu afastamento de Moraes e Dias Toffoli do STF ;

Na capital fluminense, Augusto Cury (Avante) mandou um 'abraço muito especial' a André Mendonça , do Supremo, mas sem fazer menção à crise no STF envolvendo o ministro e Moraes sobre o Caso Master.

Veja onde ocorreram manifestações contra Moraes até as 15h desta segunda-feira:

Dois grupos se concentraram no Plano Piloto da capital federal, pedindo a saída do presidente Lula e do ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF de seus cargos. Eles também criticam o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP), por não pautar o impeachment do ministro. Um dos grupos protestou em frente ao Banco Central, em Brasília.

Grupo pede afastamento de Moraes em manifestação em frente ao Banco Central, em Brasília — Foto: SSP-DF/Reprodução

A manifestação, organizada pela União dos Movimentos de Direita de Minas Gerais (UMD), ocorreu na praça da Liberdade . Segundo a organização, o ato, descrito como apartidário, teve como pautas os pedidos de "Fora Lula" e "Fora Moraes".

Lideranças da direita organizaram um ato na Praça Tamandaré , na região central da cidade, contrário ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF. O número de participantes não foi divulgado.

A mobilização foi organizada pelo Movimento Brasil (MBR) e reuniu apoiadores da direita. Os manifestantes saíram do Corredor Vera Arruda, na Jatiúca, e seguiram em direção ao Marco dos Corais, na Ponta Verde. Houve protesto contra o ministro Alexandre de Moraes e apoio ao ministro André Mendonça, ambos do STF.

Manifestantes da direita protestam, em Maceió, contra atuação de Alexandre de Moraes no STF — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

Um grupo protestou na Avenida Boa Viagem, na Zona Sul do Recife , pedindo o afastamento de Moraes. O ato ocorreu na tarde desta segunda e teve a presença de diversos candidatos a cargos nas eleições deste ano.

Manifestantes se reuniram no Farol da Barra. O protesto apoia candidatos do PL, de oposição ao governo Lula (PT), e com críticas ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes. Entre os participantes estiveram deputados federais, estaduais e vereadores do Partido Liberal.

Em São Luís, uma motocarreata organizada por movimentos de direita percorreu a capital e foi concluída no centro da cidade. Os manifestantes compareceram com camisas de cores verde ou amarelas e carregaram bandeiras do Brasil.

Protesto contra Alexandre de Moraes em Boa Viagem, na Zona Sul do Recife — Foto: Joabe Marques/TV Globo

articles.title: Trump to speak at both nights of RNC midterm convention
articles.summary: President Trump, who is already slated to speak on the first night of the Republican National Committee’s inaugural midterm convention in Dallas, will also close out the event’s second night, The Hill’s broadcast partner NewsNation confirmed Sunday. Trump is set to give the first night’s keynote address and then give closing remarks the following evening.…
articles.body:
President Trump, who is already slated to speak on the first night of the Republican National Committee’s inaugural midterm convention in Dallas, will also close out the event’s second night, The Hill’s broadcast partner NewsNation confirmed Sunday.

Trump is set to give the first night’s keynote address and then give closing remarks the following evening. Vice President Vance will deliver the second night’s keynote speech.

The president previously said in August that he will be there both nights “and rarin’ to go.”

The event, described by RNC Chairman Joe Gruters as a “Trump-a-palooza,” lists more than 100 items on its programming list — including a showcase of candidates competing in key swing districts, as well as session on banning lawmakers from trading stock, federal immigration enforcement and breaking down differences between Republican and Democratic agendas.

The event will also feature speeches from Attorney General Todd Blanche, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt. Prominent Republicans including Senate candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, House Speaker Mike Johnson (La.) and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (Wyo.) will also be in attendance.

Other lawmakers, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Sens. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) and Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) will not attend, with the latter two opting to stay on the campaign trail in their respective states, Newsweek reported .

Several reports suggest some House members chose not to attend due to an alleged $25,000 minimum RNC donation requirement for lawmakers, with the highest tier asking for $100,000. Neither Trump nor convention officials have confirmed the existence of an event attendance fee.

Democrats are aiming to run counterprogramming in Texas as the event takes place. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) announced on Friday that a four-member House delegation will go to Dallas to highlight the differing visions of both parties.

“Americans are being crushed by rising costs. Republicans don’t care—they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out of touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable,” Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) said on the social platform X.

Crow will be joined by Democratic Reps. Robert Garcia (Calif.), Madeleine Dean (Pa.) and Sydney Kamlager-Dove (Calif.). They will partner with the Texas Democratic Party and local partners for their counterprogramming in Dallas.

NewsNation reported Sunday that Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder (D) will also be Democrats hosting events in Texas during the convention.

The GOP event will be held at a point when Republicans are seeking to maintain control of a Senate seat in Texas, as Paxton is set to face off against Talarico in one of the most contested races of this election cycle. It also comes after Texas was the first to redraw its congressional maps in Republicans’ favor following Trump’s request.

Democrats have retaliated against this by redrawing their districts, most notably in California. On Thursday, Maryland’s Supreme Court ruled that a Democrat-led redistricting referendum can go on the November ballot, locking in a major victory for Democrats in the Old Line State.

articles.title: Ohio gubernatorial candidate confronted by armed man at fair
articles.summary: An armed man lunged at Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) during a Canfield, Ohio, fair on Sunday, injuring several other attendees. Acton’s campaign shared a statement after the incident, which took place at around 2:30 p.m. at the annual Canfield Fair, located in a Youngstown suburb, NBC News reported. Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office told…
articles.body:
An armed man lunged at Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) during a Canfield, Ohio, fair on Sunday, injuring several other attendees.

Acton’s campaign shared a statement after the incident, which took place at around 2:30 p.m. at the annual Canfield Fair, located in a Youngstown suburb, NBC News reported. Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office told the outlet they have 38-year-old Patrick Havas, a Canfield resident, in custody in connection to the incident.

“While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people. Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift, decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured,” campaign communications director Addie Bullock said in the statement , referring to Acton’s husband , Eric Acton.

“This kind of violence has no place in Ohio,” Bullock continued. “Dr. Acton will always stand up to this chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another.”

Acton was not hurt and remained at the fair to attend to those injured in the attack.

Mahoning County Sheriff’s spokesperson Gerry Ricciutti told NBC that Havas approached with a cellphone set up to record Acton as she spoke at the Mahoning County Democratic Party tent. He said Havas pushed through the crowd before Acton’s security detail and Ohio State Highway Patrol troopers approached him, as two people fell to the ground.

Police recovered two handguns and brass knuckle on scene, though the man did not wield any of these items in the confrontation, they said.

The incident remains under investigation, Ricciutti told the outlet. He noted Havas will face charges after investigators consult with the county prosecutor.

Acton is running to be Ohio’s next governor against Vivek Ramaswamy (R), the entrepreneur who ran for president in 2024 and was initially set to work with the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) with Tesla CEO Elon Musk before instead entering the Buckeye State’s gubernatorial race.

articles.title: Witkoff: US is confident in a ‘good resolution’ to trilateral Ukraine war talks
articles.summary: Special envoy Steve Witkoff on Sunday said the U.S. is confident that trilateral talks will result in a “good resolution” to the Ukraine war after he and President Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, met with officials in Kyiv. Sunday marked Witkoff and Kushner’s first time traveling to Kyiv to negotiate an end to Russia’s yearslong war…
articles.body:
Special envoy Steve Witkoff on Sunday said the U.S. is confident that trilateral talks will result in a “good resolution” to the Ukraine war after he and President Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, met with officials in Kyiv.

Sunday marked Witkoff and Kushner’s first time traveling to Kyiv to negotiate an end to Russia’s yearslong war in Ukraine, CNN reported . The special envoy said during a press conference that their talks were “substantive,” and that he was “confident that there’ll be a good resolution here.” The pair had met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow the day prior.

After their talks with Ukrainian officials, Witkoff told reporters that both Ukraine and Russia still “need to make some compromises,” but “we think we have the ingredients to get to that place,” The New York Times reported .

During a Sunday press conference, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the “territorial issue remains a relevant one,” pushing for resolving “complex issues … at the level of leaders.”

“But the main thing is that today we have the opportunity to discuss everything –– security guarantees, Ukraine’s future, and the prosperity plan,” Zelensky added in his remarks, translated to English and posted to his social media . “We are talking not only about security guarantees, but also about economic guarantees for Ukraine – to recover and rebuild.

The post continues, “We all understand the challenges that lie ahead once the war ends, and we are discussing them among ourselves.”

Zelensky called for Europe’s leaders to join “the third part of our negotiations,” saying he and the U.S. envoys “agreed that Ukraine, Europe and the United States will meet in the near future.”

Witkoff and Kushner met with Zelensky and other Ukrainian officials after meeting with Putin, seeking to resume stalled trilateral negotiations for a war nearing its five-year mark. The Trump administration’s efforts to help Ukraine reach a peace deal slowed after the US entered its own military conflict with Iran in February.

“One thing Steve and I really thought would be productive is to go back to the trilateral format, which we were able to do about six months ago,” Kushner said during the press conference.

The White House told The Guardian that Witkoff and Kushner had “discussed substantive plans for next steps” with Putin to end the war, with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov adding that the envoys “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement.”

Zelensky told reporters the talks focused on air defense and the creation of a “package” to support Ukraine’s energy infrastructure during the winter season. He added that the U.S. plans to increase Patriot interceptor missile production next year amid an escalation of Russian strikes in Ukrainian airspace.

Russia has deployed fast-flying jet-powered drones against Ukraine, with Zelensky calling the attacks deliberate “terror” against his people. The Ukrainian president last week warned airlines and other aviators flying through Russian airspace that his country planned to retaliate with its own aerial attacks

Ukraine and Russia agreed to pause the fighting as the envoys visited their respective capital cities, but both sides exchanged fire and intercepted the opposing army’s drones overnight Sunday. Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported one death and at least 10 wounded during separate drone attacks.

articles.title: Gonzalo Bernardos, economista, analiza el triunfo de AfD: "Han pretendido culpar de casi todos los males a los inmigrantes"
articles.standfirst: El partido de extrema derecha ha obtenido el 44 por ciento de los votos en Sajonia-Anhalt
articles.summary: El partido de extrema derecha ha obtenido el 44 por ciento de los votos en Sajonia-Anhalt
articles.body: Gonzalo Bernardos analizó la victoria del partido de extrema derecha Alianza por Alemania en las elecciones de la región germana de Sajonia-Anhalt, donde obtuvo un 44 por ciento de los votos. El economista catalán ha detallado en su cuenta personal de X, antes Twitter, los motivos por los que considera que la formación ha firmado un resultado tan contundente en las urnas. Y que ha marcado la agenda de los analistas políticos este lunes. El primer motivo del ascenso de Alianza por Alemania, según Gonzalo Bernardos, es su exposición pública. "Las redes sociales les proporciona una notoriedad que no tienen en los medios convencionales", ha comentado. Otra de las razones es la desconexión, por lo que se deduce de sus palabras, de las formaciones más tradicionales de sus votantes: "La izquierda ha olvidado a los obreros. La derecha tradicional ha olvidado al campo". El economista catalán ha señalado, además, que Alianza por Alemania no ha tenido que lidiar en gran medida con posibles comparaciones el Partido Nazi. "Un número creciente de los alemanes no los considera los herederos del Partido Nazi", ha planteado. La formación AfD nació en el año 2013, con un mensaje claro contra las políticas de económicas de la Unión Europea. Gonzalo Bernardos ha explicado otras dos razones que, para el profesor universitario y tertuliano, podrían ser esenciales para comprender el ascenso de Alianza por Alemania: "La economía va mal y muchos buenos empleos están en peligro. Han pretendido culpar de casi todos los males del país a los inmigrantes y desgraciadamente muchos ciudadanos se lo han creído". El triunfo en las urnas de Alianza por Alemania es incontestable, pero, pese a obtener el 44 por ciento de los votos y 39 escaños, no ha obtenido la mayoría absoluta. "Es un resultado maravilloso para nosotros y es un encargo para formar Gobierno", afirmó la líder nacional de AfD, Alice Weidel, tras conocer los resultados.

articles.title: It’s Labor Day, not Union Day. American workers deserve freedom of choice
articles.summary: Union bosses exploit Labor Day to push coercive policies like the PRO Act, which would repeal right-to-work laws and force compulsory union dues.
articles.body: As summer comes to an end, many Americans are looking forward to the first celebration before fall: Labor Day. A day to recognize the American worker, whose hard work and dedication make our standard of living possible. Yet every year, union bosses exploit this American tradition by stealing the spotlight from workers to argue for more coercive powers from the government. Instead of celebrating the workers they claim to "represent," union officials use this day to bullhorn rhetoric and wield political influence that protects their privileged positions. Unions today are largely built on power backed by the government. Rather than have to earn the support of individual workers, union officials wield federal law to force workers under one-size-fits-all so-called "representation," no matter how strenuously a worker might object. In the 24 states without right-to-work laws that make union financial support voluntary, union officials then legally threaten dissenting workers to "pay up or be fired." EXPLOSIVE REPORT UNEARTHS PROMINENT UNION MONEY TRAIL LABELED A 'STUNNING BETRAYAL' OF MAGA MEMBERS Even ardent supporters of forced unionism sometimes admit that union boss powers are often used to the detriment of many of the workers they purport to "represent." Take former Clinton-era Secretary of Labor Robert Reich, who has never seen a proposal for expanded union boss power he didn’t support. While a Harvard professor of business and public policy, Reich bemoaned changes in the law that "put greater weight on the voluntary aspects of unionism and de-emphasized the necessity for coercion." "In order to maintain themselves, unions have got to have some ability to strap their members to the mast," Reich explained to an Associated Press reporter. Years later, none other than former Vice President Kamala Harris similarly conceded that many workers are harmed by one-size-fits-all union monopoly contracts. As then-California attorney general, Harris filed a brief with the U.S. Supreme Court that acknowledged that "unions do have substantial latitude to advance bargaining positions that … run counter to the economic interests of some employees." FRUSTRATED BLUE-COLLAR UNION BOSSES RIP SOCIALIST POLITICIANS, WARN OF LABOR EXODUS FROM DEM PARTY Union members understand that they are frequently the victims of union coercion, which is why a recent poll by Rasmussen Media Group found that 79% of current union members agreed with the statement, "Workers should never be forced to join or pay dues to a union as a condition of employment." Nonetheless, union officials continue to push for legislation that will expand their coercive powers. For example, consider big labor’s top priority in Congress: the so-called "PRO Act." Under the guise of "reform," this bill would repeal all right-to-work laws in the majority of states, forcing compulsory union dues and monopoly bargaining on millions of people across the country. But this isn’t the only provision in the PRO Act that’s anti-worker. Another controversial provision is called the "card check" method of organizing a union. This allows union organizers to bypass the secret ballot method, which empowers workers with the final say on whether to unionize. Instead, card check lets union agents confront workers in person as many times as necessary to pressure and intimidate them into signing "authorization cards" that are then counted as "votes" for the union. Another item in the PRO Act limits workers’ ability to hold "decertification" votes to remove unions opposed by a majority of employees. These "blocks" and "bars" can keep workers trapped in forced dues for months, sometimes years, even if they unanimously oppose union "representation." No one could claim this is actually pro-worker. The ambitions of union officials today are a far cry from the wisdom and warnings of early union leaders, who sought to build union membership on a strictly voluntary basis. Even ardent supporters of forced unionism sometimes admit that union boss powers are often used to the detriment of many of the workers they purport to "represent." In a 1924 speech to delegates of the American Federation of Labor (AFL) convention, Samuel Gompers, recognized as the father of the union movement in America, said, "I want to urge devotion to the fundamentals of human liberty – the principles of voluntarism. No lasting gain has ever come from compulsion." This ideal is clearly at odds with the agenda of union officials today, who constantly seek new ways to undermine the rights of workers for political gain. articles.title: Collins’s Kavanaugh vote becomes key weapon for opponents
articles.summary: Democrats and reproductive rights groups are zeroing in on Sen. Susan Collins’s (R-Maine) vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh as a pillar of their campaign to oust her, arguing she paved the way for the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade. On Friday, Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson released an ad blasting…
articles.body:
Democrats and reproductive rights groups are zeroing in on Sen. Susan Collins’s (R-Maine) vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh as a pillar of their campaign to oust her, arguing she paved the way for the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade.

On Friday, Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson released an ad blasting Collins for voting to confirm Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch, who also voted to overturn Roe. The Kavanaugh confirmation carries greater political baggage because Collins was the deciding vote after dramatic hearings that involved claims of past sexual abuse.

In a social media video posted Friday, Jackson said, “Let’s put this idea that Susan Collins is pro-choice, you know, completely behind us.”

“That ship has completely sailed if she ever was. I mean, Kavanaugh’s certainly shown that’s something that she was willing to do,” said Jackson, also pointing to her vote this summer to confirm Erica Schwartz to be director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Jackson was referring to Schwartz’s remarks during her Senate confirmation hearing in which she told Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) that “abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.”

Before he stepped out of the race, former Democratic candidate Graham Platner also attacked Collins for voting for Kavanaugh. A 15-second ad, titled “Wrong on Kavanaugh,” accused Collins of lying when she promised to protect Roe.

Now, Jackson has picked up the same line of attack and has gathered major reproductive rights organizations behind him. Reproductive Freedom for All and the Planned Parenthood Action Fund have endorsed Jackson in the race, with the latter calling him a “reproductive rights champion.”

Reproductive Freedom for All launched a $250,000 direct-mail campaign targeting women who support reproductive freedom.

“Susan Collins’ lack of leadership and broken promises on reproductive freedom are a glaring vulnerability in this race. She promised to protect her constituents’ fundamental freedoms, and instead helped Donald Trump take them away,” the group’s president, Mini Timmaraju, said in a statement last week.

Jackson’s record on abortion complicates the discourse.

The logger and labor activist began his political career as a Republican who opposed abortion, but has said his views changed over time. Planned Parenthood gave him a 100 percent rating in terms of voting for reproductive rights as of 2021, when he was leading Maine’s Senate as a Democrat.

Discussing his evolving view, Jackson recently told The New York Times , “I’ve made mistakes early on in understanding” abortion.

Jim Melcher, professor of political science at the University of Maine at Farmington, noted Collins’s vote to confirm Kavanaugh was more than eight years ago now, and she has already won reelection once since then. This election is, however, her first since the Dobbs decision.

“I’m not sure how much more she’s going to lose from that compared to what she already lost in 2020. I think those people that voted against her for that reason will continue to do so. But I’m not sure it’s going to lead to fresh opposition,” Melcher said.

“It makes sense for Jackson to remind voters of that. Maine, broadly speaking, is a relatively pro-choice state. That’s something that she’d always highlighted about her campaign, so it makes sense for Democrats to talk about this,” he added.

Collins’s team maintains that the senator’s pro-choice record speaks for itself. Her supporters point out that she also voted for all three sitting Democratic Supreme Court justices, as well as Chief Justice John Roberts, all of whom voted against overturning Roe.

“These partisan groups just don’t know what to do about Maine. First, they had to rationalize supporting Graham Platner, who blamed women for their own rapes and had to drop out after a rape allegation,” Blake Kernen, communications director of Collins’s reelection campaign, told The Hill.

“Now they are stuck with Troy Jackson, who was not only Graham Platner’s strongest supporter, but who spent 12 years in elected office as a staunch opponent of reproductive rights and who bullied his female colleagues when he was Senate President.”

Kernan was apparently referring to an incident in which Jackson reportedly frightened a female lawmaker when he threw a water bottle during a tense meeting.

Collins has consistently stated she does not regret voting for Kavanaugh.

“When Roe v. Wade fell because of Susan Collins’s vote to put Brett Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court, Troy Jackson got to work protecting abortion rights in Maine, helping pass some of the strongest protections in the country,” Jackson campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad said.

“Even now, Collins still proudly says she doesn’t regret her vote that helped overturn Roe. While she keeps making excuses for the damage she caused, Troy will keep fighting to repair it and restore abortion rights nationwide.”

Collins, who has been in the Senate since 1996, is considered one of the most vulnerable Republicans in this election cycle. But Jackson is facing a significant disadvantage in funding . Melcher predicted the race will likely be “very close again, and be very expensive.”

“Collins still has followers that are very devoted to her and will show up. There are people who are very enthusiastic about her, but her popularity is not where it was 10 years ago, and I think a lot of it is over the abortion question and about whether or not she’s done enough to satisfy some people about being resistant to Donald Trump,” Melcher said.

articles.title: NFL football is back: 5 things to watch on and off the field
articles.summary: NFL football returns this week, and millions of fans are gearing up to lock in on another season of the country’s most popular pro sports league. The 2026 campaign arrives at a time when fans are paying more than ever to attend games in person, streaming platforms are becoming the go-to way to watch your…
articles.body:
NFL football returns this week, and millions of fans are gearing up to lock in on another season of the country’s most popular pro sports league.

The 2026 campaign arrives at a time when fans are paying more than ever to attend games in person, streaming platforms are becoming the go-to way to watch your favorite team, and gambling has embedded itself as a prominent feature of the weekly game-day experience for many.

Here are five things to watch for this NFL season, both on and off the gridiron.

The NFL is expected to be the largest driver of audiences for any media company with rights to show its games.

An increasing number of the league’s media partners comprises streaming platforms like Netflix and Amazon, which are using rights to show top NFL games in primetime and on holidays as a way to drive subscriptions and lure blue-chip advertisers.

How the NFL does business with media companies, however, is raising concern for some in the federal government.

Reports surfaced this summer suggesting the Department of Justice is considering probing the NFL over what critics say is anticompetitive behavior in its dealmaking with major media companies.

This year, it will be more expensive than ever to watch the NFL, with fans who wish to see every game needing to sign up for as many as a half dozen streaming services and paying more than $1,000 for the season to do so.

The rising costs comes as lawmakers on Capitol Hill and federal regulators have floated a revamp of the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, a law created explicitly with the NFL in mind that grants teams the ability to collectively license the sponsored telecasts of their games to national broadcast networks.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) earlier this year put forth a bill she is calling the For the Fans Act, a law that would regulate how the NFL negotiates and makes its media deals.

“Gigantic streaming services and big sports leagues have created a complicated and expensive maze of subscriptions that either stop fans from watching their teams altogether or gouge fans to simply watch the teams they love,” Baldwin said in introducing the legislation. “It shouldn’t take ten different subscriptions and a second mortgage to watch sports.”

10 years after Kaepernick, league navigates culture wars

It’s been a decade since former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick took a knee during the national anthem before games, igniting a national conversation about race, police brutality and the power of political speech in pro sports.

Kaepernick started a social justice movement among NFL players that season and sparked intense social discourse as President Trump ran for the Oval Office in 2016.

It led the league to double down on its efforts to embrace and promote diversity while it also tried to avoid turning off fans angered by the sideline protests.

A league that features only three Black head coaches, the NFL is currently being sued by Brian Flores, a Black coach who alleges the league is not following its self-imposed Rooney Rule, which dictates teams must consider minority head coaches in the hiring process.

The NFL continues to project equality and inclusion as priorities for its workforce, more than 50 percent of which is made up of nonwhite athletes.

The league confirmed it will again allow clubs to stencil phrases like “End Racism” or “Choose Love” in end zones this fall, displays that have irked some conservatives who say they are inherently political and unnecessary.

Kaepernick, who argues he was blacklisted by NFL owners because of his social justice protests, is set to publish a new memoir this month, which could potentially restart debate about the NFL and its place in broader conversations about race relations in the U.S.

The NFL has for years been working to branch out into markets outside of the United States.

The league will hold a record nine games in seven different countries this season, including first-ever games played in cities such as Melbourne, Paris and Rio de Janeiro.

Interest in the NFL remains dwarfed by supporter engagement in global soccer clubs overseas, but many attribute the league’s steadily growing popularity in countries such as England and Germany to the growth of streaming platforms.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has not ruled out the possibility the league could soon add an international team to its ranks, and many have speculated a major European city like London could host a Super Bowl in the coming years.

How well the NFL performs in its international games is something many franchise owners are surely watching closely, and a profitable showing overseas this fall could accelerate the league’s ambitions outside the U.S.

Commanders look to break through ahead of new stadium build

It has been a whirlwind of a few seasons for football fans in Washington, D.C., who saw their home team sold to billionaire Josh Harris and draft one of the NFL’s most dynamic young quarterbacks in Jayden Daniels all within the last five years.

The Commanders, which currently play home games in the nearby Maryland suburbs, are in the midst of a push to construct a new state-of-the-art stadium on the site of the old Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Stadium.

Local leaders and the club continue to negotiate how to pay for the new construction project, which is expected to come with a price tag of more than $3 billion.

Major points of contention between the two sides remain, like how to best transport fans to games, the impact the project will have on local businesses and neighborhoods and even what the stadium will be called.

President Trump, who became the first sitting U.S. president to attend an NFL regular season game last fall, has said he would like to see the Commanders’ new home named after him, a suggestion the team has not publicly weighed in on.

With next year’s NFL draft slated to take place on the National Mall, D.C. is starting to set itself apart as a key market for the league.

And it’s a market where the president likes to be seen spotlighting sports, such as the UFC fight at the White House and the IndyCar race through the mall.

The Seattle Seahawks kick off their Super Bowl defense on Wednesday night with a primetime rematch of last year’s title game against the New England Patriots, a showdown set to be broadcast on NBC for an audience of millions.

However, the Seahawks aren’t the only West Coast team expected to be a powerhouse this fall.

The Los Angeles Rams got a major boost this summer when star defensive tackle Aaron Donald announced he was coming out of retirement to rejoin his old squad on a one-year contract.

Donald’s return underscores the Rams’ win-now mindset, and he’ll join star defensive lineman Myles Garrett, another key offseason signing for the Rams along with former Kansas City Chiefs cornerback Trent McDuffie, whom the team added to its secondary during the offseason.

Some around the league say Rams general manager Les Snead has constructed one of the team’s best rosters in years, while the club’s billionaire owner, Stan Kroenke, made a splash last week by purchasing the MLB’s Los Angeles Angels, adding to his growing sports portfolio.

This year’s Super Bowl will be held at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., adding an extra incentive for the Rams to go all the way in 2026.

In the AFC, sportsbooks list quarterback Josh Allen’s Buffalo Bills and Lamar Jackson’s Baltimore Ravens to be favorites to win that conference.

The San Francisco 49ers are also seen as a potential offensive juggernaut in 2026, setting the stage for the NFC West to feasibly send three teams to the playoffs and give itself a solid chance of bringing home another Lombardi Trophy next February.

It has been a wild few days for Los Angeles sports, which saw the MLB’s Angels sold to Kroenke and the Clippers hit with some of the most punishing sanctions in NBA history over a scheme to circumvent the salary cap to acquire Kawhi Leonard in 2024. With the Rams beginning another quest for a Super Bowl this week and the Dodgers trying to set aside questions about the future of the club’s ownership group as they prep for a likely World Series run, sports buzz in Southern California should be at a fever pitch in the coming months.

The Southeastern Conference last week sued Louisiana State University and the school’s head football coach Lane Kiffin over what it alleges was “a deliberate and coordinated campaign to recruit professional athletes to play football for LSU during the 2026-27 season.” The suit gets to the heart of issues Congress is trying to address with the Protect College Sports Act. Legendary coach Nick Saban cut a TV ad for the bill that ran during Week 1 of the college football season over Labor Day weekend.

A judge presiding over a lawsuit that seeks to stop the Trump administration’s planned renovation of East Potomac Park and the public golf course there heard arguments from a preservation group that is concerned about recent tree removal on the property. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes indicated she’s not satisfied with arguments on either side of the case and told both government and preservationist group lawyers to rework their cases before she hears it again. Meanwhile, play continues at East Potomac Golf Links while the future of the property remains uncertain.

Jocks on The Hill: Rep. Riley Moore (R-W.Va.)

Rep. Riley Moore, a first-term member of the House and the grandson of former West Virginia Gov. Arch Alfred Moore Jr., answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“Watching now … it’s college football. Absolutely got to be college football.”

“West Virginia Mountaineers. Lifelong fan. I was actually born in Morgantown where the university is. … Last year was a building year, and we just got Rich Rod back. He’s going to do a fantastic job. It’s a really exciting year. If we go above .500, I’m happy.”

Is there an athlete you looked up to growing up?

“I’m going to basically cover every American sport with two guys, Michael Jordan and Bo Jackson.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“If it was professional football, the Dallas Cowboys. Can’t stand them.”

Why do you think sports brings people together in such politically divided times?

“Sports and football in particular come with so many heroics and just keeps you on the edge of your seat. It’s funny in an era where everyone is watching things on streaming and your kids are like, ‘Can we pause this?’ … no. This is happening right now. It keeps that live action spirit going on.”

This is a pretty charming essay from Jason Brown, who played seven years in the NFL and at one point was the highest-paid center in the NFL. Today, he owns and operates First Fruits Farm in Louisburg, N.C., and writes about how he is “still figuring out ways to grow and reinvent myself.”

Ben Sasse, a former Republican U.S. senator from Nebraska, pens a pointed op-ed for The Wall Street Journal advocating for why “American boys need to play football” despite concerns about concussions, arguing it “forms character by harnessing wild masculinity and directing it toward the good and the pure.”

If you have a fantasy football draft this week, you’ll want to check this one out : Sports Illustrated talked to a bunch of NFL executives and coaches who identified “10 breakout stars to watch for” this season.

articles.title: Prediction markets’ regulation draws closer to Supreme Court
articles.summary: Prediction markets have arrived at the Supreme Court’s doorstep. New Jersey this past week urged the justices to settle how prediction markets should be regulated, and a split among the nation’s appeals courts is increasing expectations that they may be inclined to get involved. The Trump administration is trying to push states out, hoping to keep prediction markets under…
articles.body:
Prediction markets have arrived at the Supreme Court’s doorstep.

New Jersey this past week urged the justices to settle how prediction markets should be regulated, and a split among the nation’s appeals courts is increasing expectations that they may be inclined to get involved.

The Trump administration is trying to push states out, hoping to keep prediction markets under federal control. Leading platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket agree.

But a bipartisan group of states wants to be the overseers. They say the new platforms are no different from regular gambling, which they regulate with broad control.

“It’s not just blue states or Democrats who are being opposed by the Trump administration. It’s really a states’ issue,” said Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, acting vice president of policy and government affairs at the Project on Government Oversight.

As trading volume on prediction markets explodes, it has created a massive battle among casino industry players, states, Native American tribes and federal regulators.

New Jersey has now teed up the issue for the Supreme Court for the first time after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit, in a 2-1 vote, blocked the state from enforcing its sports gambling laws against Kalshi, finding it was likely under the control of the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

The Supreme Court receives thousands of requests to take up cases annually, and it rejects the vast majority. But in its choosiness, the court looks to see whether appeals courts have entered decisions in conflict with one another on important matters.

A split is already emerging in the prediction markets’ fight as judges mull cases set to impact operations in Atlantic City and Las Vegas.

Breaking with the appeals panel in New Jersey’s case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit sided last week with Nevada regulators. It ruled the state can regulate Kalshi’s sports contracts.

One source close to the litigation told The Hill that together, the two decisions mean the issue will “probably” head to the Supreme Court.

“But it’s more of a mess than it ever was because they’re agreeing on some things and they’re disagreeing on others,” the source said.

Many legal observers agree the justices at some point will feel compelled to get involved. But some aren’t so sure New Jersey’s case is the right one, suggesting the court may want the issue to percolate more in lower courts.

“I think, ultimately, the Supreme Court will probably want to see a little bit more of the social impact of this,” said Howard Fischer, a partner at Moses Singer and a former Securities and Exchange Commission prosecutor.

At the center of the battle is whether Congress preempted states from regulating prediction markets by giving the CFTC exclusive jurisdiction to regulate “swaps” on its registered markets. Kalshi and other platforms say their sports wagers are exactly that.

But New Jersey and other states say that the platforms are just like the brick-and-mortar gambling businesses they have long had legal authority to regulate.

“Different States have made different choices on that score,” New Jersey wrote in its petition. “But Kalshi insists on a different approach—one where federalism has no place, and where the sports gambling laws must be the same in New Jersey as in Utah, so long as the company self-certifies its sports bets with the CFTC.”

Fischer said states are more equipped to regulate prediction markets, as they’ll deploy more personnel.

“Rather than have dedicated departments in every state with 10, 20, 30 or more people, you’re going to have one, or two, maybe, people at the federal level who may or may not be former employees of the prediction markets,” he said.

New Jersey’s efforts have bipartisan support. Forty-four state attorneys general sent a comment letter to the CFTC this summer saying it lacked authority to assert control over sports bets on prediction markets.

“The CFTC has long understood that States are best positioned to regulate gambling. But today, the CFTC has changed course at breakneck speed,” the letter reads.

It puts a broad swath of Republican states at odds with the Trump administration. The president has publicly called for the CFTC to regulate prediction markets. Donald Trump Jr., the president’s son, has a financial stake in Kalshi and last year joined the platform as a strategic adviser .

Only six states did not join the letter: Florida, Georgia, Missouri, New Hampshire, North Dakota and Texas.

Fischer pointed to how states gain significant tax revenues from gambling.

“If that is going to be taken away from the states, no state attorney general or governor — no matter what their political leanings — wants to lose some component of their budget,” Fischer said.

As New Jersey heads to the Supreme Court, Kalshi is not allowing customers to place wagers on its case. A source familiar with the decision said it was a voluntary move by the company and not done to comply with any legal requirements.

Polymarket, however, allows people to place wagers on whether the high court will take up a sports event contract case by the end of the year.

The court is set to consider New Jersey’s request to take up the issue at a closed-door conference once the justices return for their new term in a matter of weeks.

The legal battle does not directly concern insider trading. But as it inches closer to the Supreme Court, the issue has dominated.

On Aug. 31, Kalshi announced it was issuing its first lifetime ban , sanctioning former Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.), who was also fined after placing bets on whether he would attend Trump’s State of the Union address while posting on social media about it.

The CFTC recently announced the White House teleprompter operator who placed online bets on Trump’s speeches would pay roughly $172,000. And in April, a U.S. Army soldier was charged for allegedly using his knowledge of the top-secret operation to capture former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to place bets on Polymarket .

Hedtler-Gaudette said he was glad that platforms have begun taking action, but it isn’t appropriate to leave those decisions to self-policing.

“You want to know that the people who are on taxpayers’ dimes — essentially, government officials — are doing their job in the public interest, and they’re not using their privileged positions to enrich themselves and their friends and family,” he said.

“I think the model of trying to self-police just isn’t really effective and never has been effective in any industry,” he said.

articles.title: The media make excuses for the Senate nominee who empowered Hasan Piker
articles.summary: The problem with journalistic consistency is that sometimes it is likely to cost Democrats votes. We can’t have that.
articles.body:
The same industry that has spent 15 years warning about the radicalization of the Republican Party now wants us to apply a little nuance when discussing the Democratic Party’s devolution into its own lunatic fringes.

An effort is underway to create space between Democratic candidates and the party’s radical wing — a real murderers’ row of freaks, geeks, and fans of actual murder tied to the Democratic Socialists of America. But not too much space, mind you — lest Democrats need that very same freaky crowd’s help to defeat a Republican.

It is a ridiculous bit of political maneuvering, but certain journalists are happy to play along.

Nowhere is this absurd tightrope walk clearer than in Michigan, where U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) is said to have “distanced” himself from the fringe — including a former campaign surrogate — although he hasn’t actually condemned the extremists or otherwise risked alienating them. The surrogate in question is online streamer Hasan Piker, the hilariously misguided answer to the left’s question, “Where is our Joe Rogan?”

The irony, of course, is that Joe Rogan was the left’s Joe Rogan before they all lost their minds — and that’s how they ended up with Piker.

In April 2026, standing beside Piker, El-Sayed called it “ critical ” that Democrats engage with Piker’s audience. It was one of many joint campaign appearances. But Piker is a color-by-numbers political provocateur, prone to saying (jokingly, he claims, but you can be the judge) things such as, “We’re going to keep bringing in immigrants to this country on purpose, just so they can f— your sister and then maybe your daughter ;” “We’re going to destroy the white race;” that Luigi Mangione’s unarmed murder victim had it coming because he had committed “ social murder ;” that Hamas’s rapes in its Oct. 7, 2023 massacre in Israel don’t matter , he still prefers Hamas to Israel; and of course most famously that “ America deserved 9/11 .”

This is where matters get tricky for El-Sayed. Piker was a repugnant, upper-class nepo-baby shock jock long before the 2026 midterms. El-Sayed’s campaign team was surely aware of the streamer’s record when bringing him aboard — if not, it raises serious questions about their competence and his.

El-Sayed evidently had no issue with Piker’s baggage and gladly took him on as a campaign surrogate. The two mugged for photos at half a dozen events. Their relationship became a political liability only after the broader electorate took notice of Piker’s odious character.

El-Sayed cannot claim ignorance without looking like an idiot, a liar, or both.

Thus, with Piker now an undeniable drag on the campaign, El-Sayed is attempting to create the illusion of distance — but without actually disavowing his ally, and certainly without alienating the streamer’s audience.

After winning the Michigan primary over conventional, mainstream Democrats, El-Sayed announced he had “no plans” to stump with Piker again. The Senate candidate also began insisting that hardly any connection exists between himself and Piker, to whom he refers merely as “ a single streamer from California ,” remarking , “You would think if you turn on any media that this whole campaign is about a streamer in California.”

“I don’t want to have a conversation about a Twitch streamer in California,” El-Sayed has protested . “This is not a serious conversation.”

Elsewhere, El-Sayed has asserted , “If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you’re missing the boat” — as if he had not brought the man into his own campaign. He added later that he was “not interested in a conversation about a social media person in California.”

Yet El-Sayed has also tried to frame criticism of Piker as a “ massive effort to cancel Hasan ,” which is a bit inconsistent with his comments above. Indeed, El-Sayed consistently refuses to condemn or fully disavow Piker, pushing back on demands he do so with airy phrases like, “ I’m not here to disavow people’s views .”

So El-Sayed wants voters to ignore the advocate he brought onto the trail, all while sidestepping the reasons he has to distance himself in the first place.

This has not stopped more credulous elements of our media from helping out the El-Sayed campaign by adopting its framing, combining mild condemnations with the dismissive “streamer in California” characterization, and terming it “distancing.”

“El-Sayed distances himself from popular streamer’s comments on Israel and Jewish Americans,” claimed the Associated Press — going so far as to suggest, without any sort of evidence, that the candidate’s remarks “may have cooled the relationship.”

The Guardian reported that “in the span of two days, Abdul El-Sayed distanced himself from leftwing streamer Hasan Piker.” Semafor asserted elsewhere that El-Sayed had “put more distance between himself and Hasan Piker” by telling a reporter that he has “no plans” to stump with the “controversial” commentator. Politico, of course, claimed Republicans have “ jumped ” on the controversy.

Missing from all this coverage is any acknowledgment that El-Sayed has never condemned or disavowed Piker. Whatever distance exists between them is an illusion resting purely on the candidate’s own say-so. Missing from all this coverage is any acknowledgment that El-Sayed has never condemned or disavowed Piker. Whatever distance exists between them is an illusion resting purely on the candidate’s own say-so.

In contrast, the media almost uniformly insisted in 2022 that then–private citizen Trump was surely ideologically aligned with right-wing provocateur Nick Fuentes, despite Trump’s claims that he did not know him and had not invited him to Mar-a-Lago, and despite the absence of any evidence of a partnership. The theory rested entirely on proximity and Trump issuing only a mild rebuke of the antisemitic white nationalist.

When Fuentes arrived as an uninvited guest alongside Kanye West at Mar-a-Lago, CNN reported that the dinner proved Trump’s “continued willingness to associate with figures who have well-publicized antisemitic views.”

The Associated Press wrote at that time that Trump was “renewing attention to his long history of turning a blind eye to bigotry” by dining with a “Holocaust-denying white nationalist.” The Guardian reported that Trump “repeatedly refused to disavow” Fuentes, alleging Trump “fundamentally did not want to criticize” him for fear of alienating “a devoted part of his base.”

Those were all straight news reports, believe it or not.

To keep track, an unexpected dinner guest and a lack of full-throated condemnation sufficed as evidence of a Trump-led white supremacist coalition, Trump’s protests to the contrary notwithstanding. Meanwhile, a few defensive remarks are framed as sufficient evidence of the “distance” between El-Sayed and Piker, erasing months of joint appearances, photos, endorsements, and even a victory-night rally. Not only that, but El-Sayed even continues to defend Piker as a victim of cancel culture.

The problem with journalistic consistency is that sometimes it is likely to cost Democrats votes. We can’t have that.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Israel's ambassador says NYC’s Mamdani is ‘sowing chaos’ ahead of Netanyahu’s UN appearance
articles.summary: Israel's U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon said "instead of actually welcoming all world leaders," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani is "doing exactly the opposite."
articles.body: Israeli ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon told Fox News Digital that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is "sowing chaos" ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to the U.N. General Assembly later this month. Danon made the remark after Mamdani called on New Yorkers in July to protest when Netanyahu arrives to speak at the general debate at U.N. headquarters on Sept. 24. "No one can ignore Mayor Mamdani, you know, instead of actually welcoming all world leaders and making sure that the city will function properly, he is doing exactly the opposite," Danon said. "He is inciting, he is sowing chaos into the city. So this year, unfortunately, it will be harder for every New Yorker or every visitor because the mayor is actually calling for people to go out, to demonstrate and it will not deter us. The prime minister will come, will speak and will represent our nation," the ambassador added. ISRAELI PM BENJAMIN NETANYAHU VOWS TO VISIT NEW YORK DESPITE MAMDANI'S REPEATED CALLS FOR HIS ARREST "He is inciting, he is sowing chaos into the city. So this year, unfortunately, it will be harder for every New Yorker or every visitor because the mayor is actually calling for people to go out, to demonstrate and it will not deter us. The prime minister will come, will speak and will represent our nation," the ambassador added. Mamdani’s office, when asked by Fox News Digital if he had any plans to meet with Netanyahu while he is in town, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "I don't think the Prime Minister wants to meet with him," Danon said. Mamdani previously called Netanyahu a "war criminal" and "architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people." The Democratic socialist also acknowledged that he can't have Netanyahu arrested despite promising to do so during his mayoral campaign. When asked by a reporter in July about "What do you think that these people who are frustrated with Netanyahu should do when he arrives in New York City for the United Nations meeting," Mamdani said, "One of the bedrocks of our city is protest." "It is something that has been a part of what makes our city so special, that New Yorkers can express themselves whether they are in support or in opposition no matter on whatever topic," the Democratic socialist mayor said during the press conference on July 22. "And I’ve always said that when we respect our Constitution, we also respect our First Amendment. And here in New York City it will always be a place where you can exercise that." IRAN TRIED TO ASSASSINATE ONE OF NETANYAHU'S SONS, PRIME MINISTER SAYS Netanyahu told Fox News "Hannity" around a week later that, "I’m going to New York," and, "I'm going to speak the truth in front of this hate-spewing elected official who's pitting one group of New Yorkers against the others." Danon told Fox News Digital that "we have been involved in a war, a difficult one, a long one, and I think now we have a lot of opportunities ahead of us." "So the prime minister would also speak about what we achieved, but also about the opportunities," he said. Danon also said Israel has to "finish the job" in Gaza. "Hamas is still there. They are supposed to disarm, according to the president's plan. I hope it will take place. I hope that it will happen sooner than later because if it will not happen, we will have to do the job ourselves. But we cannot leave a terrorist organization in Gaza. There will be no future for the people of Gaza or for us if Hamas will stay in power," he continued. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think we can be very proud of our achievements. Israel is being criticized, but we walk very proud at the U.N. because we know that what we did, fighting evil, fighting Iran, fighting Hezbollah, fighting Hamas, it wasn't only our fight. We fought for the Western societies, for the Western democracies," Danon also said. "That's why we feel proud on what we achieved this year." articles.title: Sen Jim Justice finds way through Senate polarization to bring WWII hero memorial to DC
articles.summary: Jim Justice reveals how a last-minute conversation with Martin Heinrich broke a partisan logjam to pass the Hershel Woody Williams monument bill.
articles.body: Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., found a way to get something passed unanimously, despite what he rebukes as "romper-room behavior" of political polarization in the Senate. In an interview Saturday with Fox News Digital, Justice detailed how he worked around the Senate’s bitter partisan divide to get a monument honoring late World War II Medal of Honor hero Hershel "Woody" Williams onto the National Mall. "I've never seen anything like this, never in my life seen anything to where it is, it is so preposterous," Justice lamented. "You know, no one could make any sense out of what in the world is going on a lot of times." "I don't know why we don't talk to one another," he added. "I don't know why we're disrespectful to one other." DEMOCRATS BLINK AS SCHUMER HELPS GOP CLEAR KEY SHUTDOWN HURDLE Using good, old-fashioned dialogue, Justice's effort ultimately succeeded in getting his first Senate law passed for his late friend. The legislation is Justice’s first bill as a senator. It honors Williams, a West Virginia native who received the Medal of Honor for extraordinary heroism during the Battle of Iwo Jima and who was the last surviving World War II Medal of Honor recipient before his death in 2022 at age 98. The monument will honor Williams by name while commemorating Medal of Honor recipients as a whole. The House approved the measure on Aug. 31 after the Senate passed it unanimously in March. The legislation is now awaiting Trump’s signature. "We're really hopeful he's going to sign it this coming week," Justice said. "And I just said, Martin, I don’t know any way to tell it other than just to tell you the truth. And you’re a good guy. And I don’t know why in the world we just can’t talk with one another." Heinrich responded with a blunt explanation of the broader problem, Justice said. MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL Justice said the monument fight was especially important because Williams himself embodied the opposite of that kind of self-interest. articles.title: What the new NLRB majority should do for workers like me
articles.summary: NLRB’s first order of business should be to end the injustice that stopped me and my coworkers from getting rid of our union.
articles.body:
Four years ago, I worked at the first Trader Joe’s store that ever unionized. I opposed the decision, but when a majority of my coworkers voted in favor, I hoped for the best. My hopes were quickly dashed as the union’s organizers undemocratically pushed themselves into leadership roles and then bargained over pronoun pins, gender-affirming care, and abortion coverage rather than focusing on wages, benefits, and things that directly affected our job.

When a critical mass of my coworkers and I tried to decertify the union, the Biden administration’s National Labor Relations Board refused to allow a vote. I now work at a different Trader Joe’s store, but the experience still upsets me. The board’s job is to protect workers like me, and it failed.

This story was on my mind when the Senate confirmed new members to the National Labor Relations Board one month ago. For the first time in years, the board now has a 3-1 Republican majority. I believe their first order of business should be to end the injustice that stopped me and my coworkers from getting rid of our union. It is time to close the what could be called the “blocking charge” loophole.

Federal law guarantees workers the ability to hold elections, both to unionize and to remove unions through decertification. But under the Biden administration, the NLRB handed union officials the power to delay decertification elections. All a union has to do is file a charge alleging the employer violated federal law somewhere along the way, and the vote stops in its tracks. The workers’ right to a decertification election is simply taken away.

Workers who signed their names asking for the vote are made to watch as their petition sits idle. Meanwhile, the blocking charge winds through investigation and litigation — a process that can drag on for years. The union that workers wanted to remove stays in place the entire time.

In short, the question of who represents them gets answered by everyone except the workers.

This is the unjust barrier that my coworkers and I confronted at the Trader Joe’s store in Hadley, Mass. We had well over the 30 percent threshold of worker support to trigger a decertification election. We actually had 46 percent of workers sign up in support. Had we been given the secret-ballot vote we were supposed to get, I am certain we would have removed the union.

But we never got that vote because our union — Trader Joe’s United — strategically filed charges to block the vote. It alleged that Trader Joe’s had committed a slew of illegal activities, ranging from its dress code to undefined threats against workers. Most of the allegations were years old, even preceding the original unionization election. No matter, though: Biden’s National Labor Relations Board stopped the decertification election in its tracks.

This is not due process. It is a trap door built into the rules to give more power to union leaders at the expense of the workers they claim to represent. That is why, earlier this year, I co-signed a formal petition for rulemaking to the board, asking it to close this loophole. The fix is simple: let elections proceed, resolve the charges separately, and stop letting paperwork substitute for a vote.

Getting rid of blocking charges is the first thing the board should do with its new majority. But it is not the only problem the board can address.

The Biden National Labor Relations Board also tried to stop employers from speaking to workers in all-hands meetings. Union organizers can still reach me at my door or on my phone whenever they want, but the old Board told employers they don’t have the freedom to bring workers together to answer the kind of questions I had about what unionization means for a workplace. The new NLRB majority should instead support policies that allow workers to hear from both sides before they vote.

Then there is the NLRB’s Cemex decision in which the board under Biden ruled that if an employer commits an unfair labor practice during an organizing drive, a union can still be certified — even if the workers voted against it. As someone who fought for the right to have a real vote and lost that fight to procedural maneuvering, I find it difficult to accept that American workers could be organized without their vote counting at all.

Workplace democracy matters to me, because I’ve seen how it works — and how it doesn’t. If union leaders are going to represent workers, they should earn the right, and they should respect workers’ right to get rid of them, too. That’s not the system the NLRB has in place now. Rather, it has tilted the playing field against workers’ choice.

Workers across the country are waiting for a process that is actually fair. The NLRB must ensure that what happened to me and my coworkers never happens to anyone else.

Michael Alcorn is a Trader Joe’s employee and a visiting fellow at the Institute for the American Worker.

articles.title: Remember Frances Perkins this Labor Day, a champion of workers’ rights
articles.summary: Workers have never had a greater champion than Frances Perkins, and it is a shame that more Americans don’t know her by name.
articles.body:
As we continue to celebrate our country’s 250th year in 2026, we remember the American heroes who made this country what we know and love today. This Labor Day, Americans have a special opportunity to honor present-day workers alongside the people and movements from our past.

Labor Day encourages us to remember America’s labor movement and the fight for workers’ rights as industrialization turned to globalization and now to the technological age. Workers have never had a greater champion than Frances Perkins , and it is a shame that more Americans do not know her by name.

Perkins was the first woman to join a presidential Cabinet, serving in the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration as secretary of Labor for 12 years. She became Labor secretary during the Great Depression, when there were 13 million jobless Americans — a quarter of the U.S. workforce at the time.

Turning crisis into opportunity, Perkins became the longest-serving secretary of Labor in American history. It is easy to understand why: Perkins was the architect behind many of FDR’s New Deal policies. She worked tirelessly to improve the lives of everyday Americans. In her words , she “came to Washington to work for God, FDR, and the millions of forgotten, plain, common workingmen.”

Perkins’s relentless advocacy for working people ensured that policymakers considered them as they created the social safety nets and protections that would change their lives forever. Not only did Perkins help establish Social Security, which still supports tens of millions in 2026, she also rewrote the proverbial rules of the workplace. It was Perkins who established many of the workplace standards that we still rely on, including the 40-hour work week. She also drafted the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, banning child labor and establishing a minimum wage to improve living conditions.

Perkins was partly inspired to action after witnessing New York’s tragic Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire early in her career, which killed 146 workers . She watched as workers — most of them young women and immigrants — jumped to their deaths from the upper floors of the 10-story Triangle Shirtwaist Co. building in Greenwich Village, knowing that the factory exits were locked and the single fire escape was inoperable.

Following this tragedy, Perkins didn’t just hope for a better future; she worked tirelessly to make it a reality.

Her advocacy created a retirement program for workers and mandated compensation for work-related accidents, in addition to establishing an unemployment insurance program that was unimaginable just years earlier. Perkins was a vital bridge between the 18th-century ideals of the Founding Fathers and the complex realities of the 20th-century industrial economy. She showed that the Declaration of Independence is not a static document; it is a living contract between a government and its people.

Frances Perkins revolutionized our expectations for the role that government could serve in our lives. She believed her and her colleagues “evolved the ethical principle that it was not right or just that an honest and industrious man should live and die in misery.” Countless working Americans live safer lives today because of Perkins.

Nearly a century after her service as Labor secretary, Perkins’s vision continues to be a beacon for better. We honor that vision at the Frances Perkins Center in Newcastle, Maine. The Perkins Family Homestead, now the Frances Perkins National Monument, is where Perkins spent her childhood summers with her grandmother and first learned the value of hard work and caring for your neighbors. Today, Americans can visit the national monument and learn more about her legacy — hopefully positioning her as a household name alongside George Washington, Harriet Tubman and the many other figures we celebrate from our nation’s history.

This Labor Day, our mission is to honor the American workforce that built our nation’s strength, prosperity and high standard of living, while acknowledging that there is still work yet to be done. As we envision the next 250 years, we can find inspiration in the dreamers and doers who came before us.

Amanda Hatch serves as executive director of the Frances Perkins Center in Newcastle, Maine.
