articles.title: Why Tuskegee University’s new dress code matters
articles.summary: Tuskegee University president Mark A. Brown is implementing stricter dress codes and cell phone policies to help students avoid negative stereotypes and prepare for professional success.
articles.body:
President Trump’s war in Iran has no end in sight. Bond markets are flashing ominous signs. And the midterm elections are less than 60 days away.

In this time of anxiety, the dress code at Tuskegee University in Alabama might seem like a small matter. It isn’t.

Tuskegee recently told its mostly Black students to stop wearing revealing clothes to class, or at university events. School leaders also insisted they turn off cell phones in class. And the school also put a stop to students dressing down by wearing durags.

Mark A. Brown, the school’s president, said at start of the school year he is sending a clear message: He wants to end habits that hurt any Black youngster’s chances for success. He is educating young Black people to defy self-defeating images of themselves as thugs.

In refreshingly direct terms, Brown said, “The only need we feel is to prepare students to be successful: That’s it.”

As President Trump punishes diversity efforts at universities and corporations, Tuskegee’s strong message to young Black people is simple — they cannot afford any self-imposed handicaps.

Feeding stereotypes with jailhouse-inspired fashion choices is a self-imposed handicap. Feeding negative, ugly assumptions tying young Black people to crime and violence is a self-imposed handicap.

A reminder of self-imposed handicaps flashed nationwide last week with the conviction of a Black man for killing the Black rapper Tupac Shakur. The New York Times described Shakur as a “socially conscious poet on his way to becoming a cultural icon.” But he was derailed, the paper reported, as he allowed his fame to become “increasingly associated with violence and gang culture.”

The same slide into gangster life later took the life of another rapper, Christopher Wallace, better known as “Notorious B.I.G.”

Those young stars died nearly 30 years ago. But negative stereotypes about “authentic” Black life replicating jailtime are heavily promoted in rap music and fashion — the durags and pants that hang low after belts are confiscated.

Tuskegee is standing up to this lie by giving its students practice in professional dress and habits that lead to success.

Twenty years ago, I wrote a book , a New York Times best-seller, “ENOUGH,” that called out Black activists, along with educators, for not confronting negative cultural messages about Black youth in music and fashion.

I argued that too many traditional Black leaders had lost sight of the original purpose of the civil rights struggle: improving the lives of Black Americans.

With prominent voices muzzled, the popular culture continues to elevate hip hop even as it goes about normalizing the N-word, degrading Black women and celebrating the destructive fantasy of “Gangsta” life.

Hip Hop led to “Gangsta” rap and then to drill music — music whose very name evokes Black people killing Black people.

I even took that argument onto Oprah Winfrey’s show, where I confronted rapper Ice-T over rap lyrics that glorified violence and sexual degradation. One dissenter derided me as a “hip-hop scold of the highest order.”

Maybe so, but I had company. Before he became president, Barack Obama, as a U.S. senator in 2008, said too many Black men were under the influence of negative stereotypes and failing as fathers and husbands. He said they were “acting like boys instead of men … families are weaker because of it.”

As president in 2013 he spoke at Morehouse College and delivered a similarly direct message : “Be the best husband to your wife, or boyfriend to your partner, or father to your children that you can be, because nothing is more important.”

His challenge to Black America was criticized by some of the same old-guard critics I challenged in “Enough.”

They also lambasted comedian Bill Cosby for his speech at the 2004 anniversary celebration of the Supreme Court ruling ending legal school segregation in Brown v. Board of Education.

Cosby said Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Thurgood Marshall had sacrificed, even gone to jail, to fight racial segregation and open doors to success for Black America. He said modern-day white racism was not the principal reason for high rates of truancy from school and failure to graduate. The problem, he said, was that poor people “are not holding their end in this deal.”

We later learned that Cosby was in no position to lecture anyone about morality or the treatment of women. His fall from grace destroyed his credibility as a messenger.

But it did not — and does not — invalidate his message.

In fact, his words are more salient today because they are harder to hear in a world of political messages dominated by Trump. Now any call for personal responsibility in Black America gets confused with partisan politics and ideological purity. It shouldn’t be.

Standards are not racist. Discipline is not disrespectful of Black culture. Black lives do matter.

This is especially true as artificial intelligence makes the job market the most competitive it has been in decades.

Booker T. Washington, Tuskegee’s founder in the days after the Civil War, understood that education was not simply the acquisition of knowledge. It was about preparing Black students to live with independence, dignity and success.

In 2026, Tuskegee is not surrendering to popular stereotypes. It is preparing young people to win.

That is why what Tuskegee is doing today matters.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

articles.title: New Mexico governor rips Trump’s ‘New America’ post, says name ‘isn’t up for debate’
articles.summary: New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D) slammed President Trump’s recent post where he shared a map showing her state renamed as “New America.” “New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed. What is up for debate? Who’s showing up for working families,” Lujan Grisham said…
articles.body:
New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D) slammed President Trump’s recent post where he shared a map showing her state renamed as “New America.”

“New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed. What is up for debate? Who’s showing up for working families,” Lujan Grisham said in a post on the social platform X on Sunday.

“While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring. Americans are also spending more at the grocery store, losing access to health care and wondering if they’ll ever be able to afford a home,” the governor added.

On Sunday, Trump posted a map of New Mexico labeled “New America” after a debunked online hoax spread that he had signed an executive order changing the state’s name.

The map, which the president posted to Truth Social, featured a large “X” over “Mexico” in the state’s name and the word “America” below it. The White House’s official account also posted the image on X.

Trump said later Sunday evening on Truth Social that “many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA.”

“So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!!”

Trump’s Sunday posts also came in the wake of the president recently signing an executive order to rename Lake Ontario , which shares its name with a Canadian province, to “Lake America” amid trade tensions with the U.S.’s northern neighbor.

“Under Democratic leadership here in New Mexico, we’re providing families with free childcare and college, protecting access to health care and investing in housing. While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work,” Lujan Grisham said in her Sunday X post.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: The 2028 Democratic presidential nominee will likely be a governor
articles.summary: Governors have both the responsibility to deliver for their constituents and the power to do so.
articles.body:
The race for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination is underway and will intensify immediately following the 2026 midterm elections. Several Democrats have taken the early steps needed to begin what will likely be a multi-billion-dollar undertaking should he or she become the party’s nominee.

What is driving this likely multi-candidate and contentious contest is an overwhelming belief among political prognosticators that 2028 will be another in a series of change elections since President Trump’s 2016 victory. Democrats sense that Trumpism is losing altitude and voters will be looking for something very different. And those candidates who have a record of delivering real change are what voters want.

Presidential candidates who hail from the halls of Congress are unlikely to succeed. The Gallup poll finds just 16 percent of Americans approve of the job Congress is doing. And congressional Democrats don’t fare much better. Just 18 percent of all voters and 42 percent of self-identified Democrats approve of the way they are doing their job.

For Democratic members of Congress showing early signs of presidential ambition — Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.J.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) — this is hardly a promising start.

Once upon a time, being a member of Congress offered a promising path to victory. During the Cold War congressional experience, especially in foreign affairs, was something voters valued, and they chose candidates who were well-versed in those issues.

John F. Kennedy, Lyndon B. Johnson, Hubert H. Humphrey and George McGovern all won their party’s presidential nominations . Congressional Republicans also scored victories at their conventions : Richard Nixon, Barry Goldwater and Gerald Ford carried the Republican standard into November. As the Cold War Atomic Clock ticked closer to midnight, voters wanted someone with foreign policy experience to have his finger on the nuclear trigger.

Things have changed. In an era where voters are tired of pie-in-the-sky promises and failures to deliver, producing actual results matters most. This year, for example, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) is cruising to victory on the promise that he “ gets s— done .”

As Shapiro’s example illustrates, governors have both the responsibility to deliver for their constituents and the power to do so. He and Democratic Govs. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, Gavin Newsom of California and Wes Moore of Maryland appear on virtually every list of possible nominees. Each has written the mandatory book (or books) telling their respective stories and why they might be the best pick. And a governor who hails from a state that either Democrats must win, or haven’t won in decades, is an asset when the Electoral College remains the arbiter of presidential success.

Fundamentally, the presidency is an executive position, and gubernatorial experience is an asset. For example, Ronald Reagan biographer Lou Cannon writes that Reagan’s eight years as governor were essential preparation for the presidency. At a dinner honoring the nation’s governors in 1981, Reagan remarked that he found little difference between being a governor and being a president.

Some of the founding fathers thought governors would make good presidents. At the 1787 Philadelphia Convention, Massachusetts delegate Elbridge Gerry suggested that state governors should appoint the president because they could best determine the qualities the chief magistrate must possess.

Gerry’s idea was not approved, but a variant of it was practiced initially. Throughout much of the 19th century and into the early 20th century, several governors went from their statehouse mansions to the White House. Herman Talmadge, a former governor and later U.S. senator, once said , “A governor makes decisions and executes them. A senator makes decisions and talks about them.”

After a series of disappointing presidencies, Alexis de Tocqueville wrote : “After having had excessive pride, we have fallen into a humility that is just as excessive; we thought we could do everything, and now we think we can do nothing.”

Today, a similar sentiment has taken hold. In 2000, the late Wilson Carey McWilliams described what he called this new politics of disappointment : “Most Americans, looking backward, find it hard not to see a long, slow slide: real wages declining, society deteriorating, gaps widening between old and young, and rich and poor, the hopeful integrationism of the civil rights movement turned into a bitter politics of race.”

More than a quarter century later, little has changed. Unless the next president can reduce the income gap, provide better healthcare, childcare, and housing and lift the nation from the depths of the culture wars to a higher plane, the malaise that Jimmy Carter spoke of so long ago will surely become a permanent feature of our body politic. Electing a governor might just be the tonic the nation needs.

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at The Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, co-authored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “ Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics. “

articles.title: Erika Kirk recounts Usha Vance’s advice after husband’s death: ‘Her words are seared into my heart’
articles.summary: Erika Kirk, the wife of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, in a new New York Times opinion piece published Monday discussed the words she recounted receiving from second lady Usha Vance after her husband’s death. In her essay, Erika Kirk says that the day after her husband was fatally shot, she had a conversation…
articles.body:
Erika Kirk, the wife of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, in a new New York Times opinion piece published Monday discussed the words she recounted receiving from second lady Usha Vance after her husband’s death .

In her essay , Erika Kirk says that the day after her husband was fatally shot, she had a conversation with Vance.

“I don’t know how I’m going to do this,” Kirk says of her conversation with Vance, to which the second lady replied, “You know when you’re on an airplane with your kids, and you’re going to land in 15 minutes, but the kids are going crazy, screaming, throwing things, and then the plane lands, and the kids relax, and everything is fine again?”

“That’s how it will be. Just get through the next 15 minutes,” Vance told Kirk, according to her Times piece.

Kirk wrote that Vance’s “words are seared into my heart.”

“Grief is strange. Time continues even when every part of you wants it to pause or, better yet, rewind. But the people we love who have passed on would not want us to spend the rest of our lives trying to rewind. At first, I needed to survive the next 15 minutes. Over time, I’ve realized that Charlie would want me to live them,” she added.

Charlie Kirk was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, while giving a speech at Utah Valley University.

During a memorial service honoring her husband in late September last year, Erika Kirk broke down at one point as she said she forgave the suspect who allegedly shot and killed him. Kirk spoke at length about her husband’s mission and the centrality of religion in her family during the event.

“I love you Charlie, baby. And I will make you proud,” Kirk said when ending her speech, to which the audience responded with strong applause.

Last month, Turning Point USA announced that Charlie Kirk will be honored at an event Thursday on the Utah Valley University campus, near where he was shot.

articles.title: It’s a tough time for unions in the age of Trump — cities and states can help
articles.summary: Say yes to Labor Day picnics and barbeques and parades. But also say yes to building more and stronger unions.
articles.body:
On Labor Day, it’s worth considering: how can we bolster unions in the U.S.?

Unions have a better public image today than they have in generations. Yet because of fierce corporate opposition and weak federal laws, the share of workers who are union members is way down — around 10 percent of workers nationwide.

Workers themselves have always led the way in building collective power, but laws and government shape the landscape. It’s nice when political leaders attend a Labor Day picnic or parade, and it’s moving when they wax eloquent about the dignity of work. But right now, we need so much more.

Sadly, the Trump administration is taking a bat to workers’ rights, reducing wage theft enforcement , shrinking the Department of Labor and weakening the National Labor Relations Board, which enforces workers’ right to unionize. With Washington hostile and the Supreme Court’s right-wing majority averse to working people, that leaves cities and states.

Some Democratic state leaders have betrayed working people , but many others are trying mightily. Unfortunately, federal law sharply limits their ability to regulate labor relations. New York learned this in July when a federal court blocked a new law granting additional power to the state in this area.

The needle-threading maneuver, then, is for state and local governments to find ways to boost unionization that won’t get slapped down in federal court. Plenty of labor experts have proposed creative and innovative ideas .

Here’s a new one: a deceptively simple, under-the-radar idea that requires no legislation and costs almost nothing. State and local governments can help people unionize by simply helping to organize workers. Specifically, they can host meetups between workers and local unions, and they can teach the public about unions.

For starters, do you know how you would form a union in your workplace? Most people have no idea. Perhaps the most important move is just to bring workers and unions together. State and local officials could, as a form of constituent services, host hometown gatherings between workers and local unions. Worker centers and groups like the Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee could be included, too.

Government does this kind of thing — connecting constituents with community resources — all the time. Think about health and wellness fairs, for example, or job fairs that connect employers and job seekers.

Imagine if New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani or Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) personally hosted a monthly or quarterly union fair, where local unions and potential new members could meet up, organized by neighborhood or industry. Between fairs, government staffers could connect workers interested in unionizing with appropriate contacts at unions in their industry.

The beauty of this approach is that you don’t have to be a governor or a mayor to do it. You don’t need to be nationally known, wildly popular or even particularly charismatic. A union fair could be held by city council members, state legislators, county commissioners or a state labor secretary. All you need is warm coffee, stale pastries, a space to meet, and some good old-fashioned organizing chops.

State and local governments can also educate workers about unionizing. People typically know little about workplace rights, and even popular culture has a void. When is the last time you saw a TV show featuring a union campaign? I can think of just one — thank you, “Superstore.”

California and New Jersey have passed laws requiring workers’ rights education in public high schools. Cities and states could do this as well. They could also include local union contact information (with permission) on government websites, with descriptions of whom the unions serve, just as government websites often link to nonprofits and organizations that serve the community.

State and local governments could run public service ad campaigns, with QR codes linking to more information, or to surveys about people’s working conditions. Agencies can also use existing touchpoints: job seekers are ideally situated to receive know-your-rights information, as well as workers filing wage theft complaints .

To be sure, even these simple proposals will meet resistance. Some Chamber of Commerce somewhere will make a fuss if a mayor organizes a meetup with unions, or if a state labor department posts “how to form a union” on its website. They will say it is biased or unfair, even though business interests already have vastly disproportionate access to government leaders. They might even sue.

But educating workers and organizing meetups aren’t the kind of “regulation” preempted by federal labor law. What would corporate opponents argue in court? That they’re legally entitled to employees who are unaware of their rights and have never talked with a union representative?

Even worker-hostile states couldn’t stop local government from this kind of action: educating people about their rights is a matter of free speech, and meetups involve the right of assembly.

Opposition could also arise among well-intentioned public servants worried that this involves government inappropriately taking sides. But business interests already have disproportionate access to government at all levels. And civil society organizations civil society organizations, including organized labor, are a bedrock of strong democracies. Remember, unions don’t just help members; they reduce income inequality , improve mobility for members’ children and increase civic participation . Even with their current low density, unions are the largest civil society player standing up, at scale, for all of us who don’t belong to the ultra-wealthy class.

The current crisis on labor rights calls for a multi-faceted approach. Some states, most recently Oregon and Washington , allow striking workers to receive unemployment insurance . Several states have created three-party boards giving unions and workers a seat at the table in establishing rules for a whole industry. We need all of this and more.

But sometimes, untapped potential lies right under our noses. So say yes to Labor Day picnics and barbeques and parades. But also say yes to building more and stronger unions. Even without passing new laws, state and local governments can do this by, quite simply, helping workers organize.

Terri Gerstein is the director of the NYU Wagner Labor Initiative at NYU’s Robert F. Wagner Graduate School of Public Service.

articles.title: Where is ‘King of Debt’ Trump when we need him on the national debt?
articles.summary: The United States is now well beyond responsible management of the debt, and my party has lost its willingness to recommend the hard choices needed to control it.
articles.body:
In 2016, then Republican Presidential candidate Donald Trump arrogantly proclaimed that he was the “ King of Debt ,” and boasted that he could eliminate the then $19 trillion national debt in eight years — presuming, as he did, that he would have two consecutive terms in office.

Ten years later, the Republican president and the Republican Congress have allowed the national debt to exceed $40 trillion . That debt is roughly 120 percent of our Gross Domestic Product, or GDP.

Let those simple facts to sink in: It is more than $230,000 in debt for every taxpayer.

A modest level of debt is not harmful. In fact, it’s necessary for a government’s capital investments and survival in times of crises, like the dot-com bubble or the COVID pandemic. But when the crisis passes or the investment pays off, a responsible and reliable government then pays the debt down while reinvesting in its future.

When the government fails to act responsibly in robust times, a nation’s economic strength is slowly and surreptitiously diminished. It is not, however, unpredictable. The danger is that unless leaders responsibly focus attention on the issue and honestly recommend steps to reduce the deficit, economic damage occurs in the shadows. It’s like termites eating away at a building. Those inside don’t know that the building is weakening until it is too late. Currently, the termites are embedded in the building, and they are eating the foundation at an alarming pace.

When Sen. Jack Danforth (R-Mo.), the founder of my organization, and Sen. Bob Kerrey (D-Neb.) chaired the Bipartisan Commission on Entitlement and Tax Reform in 1994, they emphasized then that “America is at a fiscal crossroads,” and failure to take action would “threaten the financial future of our children and our nation.”

At the end of fiscal 1994, the national debt was $4.6 trillion. The U.S. is now well beyond responsible management of the debt, and my party has lost its willingness to recommend the hard choices needed to control it.

The Committee for a Responsible Budget estimates that the national debt increased by $8.4 trillion in President Trump’s first term. It increased roughly the same amount under former President Joe Biden. So far, it has increased about half that amount in under 20 months of Trump’s second term.

Truly, neither party has been willing to make responsible decisions about addressing runaway debt. But it is the Republican majorities in Congress and a Republican president who have controlled the Executive and both houses of Congress in President Trump’s second term. And yet, the debt accumulation has not slowed at all. In fact, it has only increased with the “King of Debt” at the helm. And that is unforgivable.

Last month, the Wall Street Journal blamed both parties’ spending for the ballooning debt. The editors argue that revenue has increased significantly while spending has metastasized and that the need to cut spending to tame the deficit is simply unavoidable.

The fact is that when asked, the president expresses concern about the national debt and confidence that he can eliminate it on one hand, yet, on the other hand, endorses budgets and takes executive actions that do just the opposite. He repeatedly emphasizes that on the one hand we need to spend significantly more on defense, but on the other hand, proceed with cutting revenues in order to stimulate growth. He then pursues foreign and security policies that fail to achieve the strategic aims of the country, while increasing the national debt exponentially.

The math just doesn’t add up. What is accurate is that the people of America are paying for the massive increases in spending without receiving any positive results.

Entitlement spending growth, increased defense costs and rising interest payments are the driving forces pushing annual deficits sky high and growing national debt. There is no magic pill that will reduce that spending without courage and bipartisan decisions embraced by the nation’s leaders. That’s the price of leadership and one thing the country can afford.

In the August 1994 report , the former senators said that if we did nothing, “Americans 10, 15 and 20 years from now will ask why we had so little foresight.” As the national debt crosses the inconceivable $40 trillion mark, Americans should be asking this question and demanding action.

Where’s the “King of Debt” when the country needs him?

Marc Racicot is the national co-chairman of Our Republican Legacy . He is a former governor of Montana and chair of the Republican National Committee.

articles.title: Trump’s DC makeover: What to know
articles.summary: The Supreme Court last week cleared the way for President Trump to continue construction of a massive ballroom replacing the White House’s East Wing, removing a major legal hurdle for one of his several beautification projects around Washington, D.C. Since returning to office for a second term, Trump has launched a sweeping campaign to transform…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court last week cleared the way for President Trump to continue construction of a massive ballroom replacing the White House’s East Wing, removing a major legal hurdle for one of his several beautification projects around Washington, D.C.

Since returning to office for a second term, Trump has launched a sweeping campaign to transform the nation’s capital as part of his efforts to “Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Again.”

The projects — which range from the estimated $400 million ballroom and a 250-foot triumphal arch to smaller-scale renovations of parks and monuments across the city — have sparked concern from preservationists, and in some cases, prompted litigation to block their progress.

Here’s what you need to know about the current status of the president’s D.C. makeover.

Trump said the planned 90,000-square-foot project, which includes a drone-launching pad and underground military complex, is necessary for national security purposes and would provide a much larger venue for state dinners.

While a final decision on the legality of the ballroom has yet to be reached, construction will be allowed to continue following the Supreme Court ruling, as a 250-person crew works at the site 20 hours a day, seven days a week, according to court records.

“We have hundreds of happy construction workers in D.C. busily doing their job building the finest Ballroom/Military complex anywhere in the World,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Wednesday.

He continued, “It is important to remember, the Ballroom is a 400 Million Dollar gift to America!”

The National Trust for Historic Preservation successfully challenged the ballroom’s legality in the lower courts, arguing that Trump did not receive the necessary approval to move forward with the project.

The project is being financed in part through private donations from corporations and wealthy individuals, which has drawn concerns over possible conflicts of interest.

In June, government watchdog group Public Citizen published an analysis finding that 14 of the ballroom’s 27 known corporate donors received new or increased federal contracts worth more than $50 billion within the first six months of this year.

Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch is moving closer to construction after the Interior Department announced Thursday that excavation at the site will begin within the next two weeks .

The massive white and gold arch will be built at an entrance to the city, and Trump said he plans to make it the “biggest” in the world, similar to the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

A recent federal assessment determined that the arch would adversely affect dozens of historical sites around the capital, obstructing views of iconic Washington landmarks such as the Washington Monument, the Lincoln Memorial and the Capitol.

Trump’s proposed triumphal arch received pushback from Democrats, who argue that the project did not receive approval from Congress and was therefore illegal .

Three Vietnam War veterans sued the Trump administration to block the construction of the arch earlier this year, citing the lack of congressional approval and concerns that it would obstruct the view of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district includes the Arlington National Cemetery, said Thursday that the “plainly illegal” arch was not ready to be built.

“Burgum and the Trump Administration are disregarding the risks and rushing this towering monument to Trump’s vanity because they believe Republicans will get crushed in November,” he said in a statement, referring to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

Shortly after Trump returned to office, crews in D.C. tore down the large yellow “Black Lives Matter” mural painted near the White House.

The mural was commissioned by D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser (D) in 2020 at the height of protests following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis, in rebuke of Trump’s deployment of federal law enforcement during his first term to clear protesters.

The $4.8 million installation was removed in the face of pressure from Republicans in Congress, who threatened to withhold transportation funding unless the city removed the mural and renamed the two-block stretch “Liberty Plaza.”

The Trump administration’s renovations at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are ongoing after an algae outbreak tinted the water green and the pool’s newly installed “American flag blue” paint began to peel away.

The president claimed that the pool had been vandalized and directed his Department of Justice (DOJ) to crack down on alleged culprits, but the DOJ later dropped charges against several people who had been accused of vandalizing the iconic water feature last month, including a former Olympic canoeist .

U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, the former Fox News personality and top Trump ally, blamed the Department of the Interior for the initial charges against canoeist David Hearn. Her decision initially led to tensions with Trump.

The project also faced criticism after the federal government awarded no-bid contracts to two firms with ties to Trump.

Atlantic Industrial Coatings — the Virginia-based firm responsible for installing the pool’s new base layer — had previously done work for one of the president’s golf clubs. The same company has been tasked with handling the repairs, which the president said last week were “almost completely fixed.”

Trump has pushed to include his name on several iconic landmarks during his second term, including at the Kennedy Center.

Last year, the president fired half of the center’s traditionally bipartisan board, appointed himself as the new chair and handpicked administration allies to serve on the center’s governing body.

Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty (Ohio), an ex officio member of the center’s board, sued the Trump administration in December over the proposed name change, calling it a “flagrant violation” of the Constitution.

Workers added the president’s name to the building facade but later removed the letters amid the ongoing legal battle.

The center’s new board has also made other physical alterations to the performing arts venue’s campus, directing the removal of a 24-foot sculpture named “Blue” that was gifted to the Kennedy Center in 2019 on Wednesday. A Kennedy Center spokesperson told The Hill the artwork would be relocated at the discretion of a foundation dedicated to the sculpture’s creator.

In May, Trump unveiled the location of a “National Garden of American Heroes” in West Potomac Park, saying the garden would transform a “BARREN field of Prime Waterfront Real Estate along our Mighty Potomac River” into “one of the World’s most beautiful public spaces.”

The statue garden will feature 250 Americans whom the garden intends to honor as part of the administration’s celebration of America’s 250th birthday this year, including the Founding Fathers, basketball star Kobe Bryant, Walt Disney and the late “Jeopardy!” host Alex Trebek.

But the garden’s construction has yet to come to fruition after being stalled by more legal challenges to the federal government’s use of public land in D.C.

A group of preservationists sued the Trump administration over the garden, arguing it was violating federal laws including the Commemorative Works Act, which prohibits placing new monuments or commemorative works on the National Mall without congressional approval.

The Trump administration’s efforts to restore several fountains across the nation’s capital have been more widely welcomed by D.C. residents.

Water began flowing through a cascading fountain in the city’s historic Meridian Hill Park for the first time in seven years, following a $4 million renovation project’s completion in July. However, maintenance crews returned to work on the fountain less than two weeks after its reopening, as sediment from the fountain’s old pipes turned the water a murky brown color.

Additionally, workers restored the Christopher Columbus Memorial Fountain outside of Union Station in an $11.79 million rehabilitation project. The administration said the fountain had not been in working condition for nearly two decades.

“Columbus Circle is a historic front door to Washington, D.C. and thanks to @POTUS, today it is once again ready to welcome the public!” Burgum wrote in a social media post following the fountain’s reopening in May.

The Trump administration has repeatedly accused the Smithsonian Institution’s leadership of “ideological activism,” warning it could cut off federal agencies from working with the museum complex if its concerns are not resolved.

In a July executive order , Trump ordered the installation of disclaimers outside of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History to warn visitors that some of its exhibits did not match his version of the nation’s past.

The president accused the museum of treating America’s history “as a ‘prime tool’ to advance ideas of social justice and the radical transformation of our society,” citing the findings of a White House report on the museum’s exhibits.

The museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, told lawmakers in July that the report failed to “fairly or accurately” depict the museum’s exhibits and stressed the museum “does not take sides in America’s political debates.”

Additionally, the Smithsonian Institution’s National Portrait Gallery removed information earlier this year about Trump’s two impeachments from a plaque next to his presidential portrait in the museum.

Previous text next to his portrait noted that Trump was impeached on charges of incitement of insurrection related to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.

The president’s decision to pave over the Rose Garden was among his most controversial changes to the White House grounds. The new outdoor space reopened last year, with picnic tables and yellow umbrellas that bore an unmistakable similarity to those at his Mar-a-Lago residence’s pool patio.

Trump has utilized the space to host tech and business leaders , GOP members of Congress and others at the executive residence. This year, several gifted statues of the Founding Fathers were added to the patio space.

On Wednesday, the president hosted a group of vulnerable Republican lawmakers in the Rose Garden for dinner as the GOP fights to maintain their control of Congress in the midterm election this fall.

articles.title: We made workplace safety a priority once. We can again.
articles.summary: Despite historical progress under the Occupational Safety and Health Act, current workplace safety efforts face significant challenges due to stagnant regulations, insufficient inspection resources, and evolving labor structures.
articles.body:
This May, a chemical tank ruptured at a paper mill in Longview, Wash ., killing 11 people. The tragedy marked the rare occasion of workplace safety making it into the national news. Most workplace tragedies, sadly, never get that attention, even though more than 5,000 people die from accidents at work every year .

Even more hidden from view are the estimated 135,000 that die from occupational diseases tied to exposures to dangerous chemicals and other factors. Millions are injured, some never able to work again.

We have come to accept this slow daily trickle of fatalities and injuries as inevitable and the cost of doing business. We ignore the urgent protections workers need and the reality that we could do more to prevent these tragedies and the destruction they cause to families and communities.

We didn’t always turn a blind eye. We once made worker safety a national priority and both parties saw the urgency. President Richard Nixon signed the Occupational Safety and Health Act in 1970 , establishing OSHA after over 300 coal miners died in 1968. Since then, workplace deaths dropped from more than 30 per day to about 15 today, even as the workforce has more than doubled. But our progress stalled more than a decade ago.

Urgency has been replaced with negligence. In 1980, OSHA had nearly 15 inspectors for every million covered workers. Today, it has fewer than six , resulting in about 740 federal inspectors overseeing 11.6 million worksites . We have also fallen woefully behind in updating protections. Former OSHA Director David Michaels estimates that 90 percent of our chemical exposure limits were developed in the 1960s . Most chemicals used in the workplace have no exposure limits.

The Mine Safety and Health Administration went for more than 50 years without updating the exposure limit for silica, the primary culprit behind black lung. A rule finally updating that standard was issued in 2024, but its implementation is now delayed , with little assurance that it will move forward.

Penalties for employers for deaths and injuries are often a slap on the wrist. Fines for serious safety violations are $4,700 on average and for fatalities, only about $20,000. One employer paid a more than $100,000 after illegally employing a 15-year-old who died on the first day at work. Just 144 workplace fatalities have been referred for criminal prosecution in the whole history of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, despite nearly half a million deaths on the job. Michaels also recently wrote about a failing workers compensation system that allows employers to shirk the costs of workplace injuries.

New challenges are being dismissed. A long-awaited heat standard is being blocked even as temperatures soar. A new wave of lung disease among countertop workers is being ignored. And no federal workplace violence standard exists.

Our economy has changed significantly since the Occupational Safety and Health Act passed. The rise of gig workers, independent contractors, temporary staffing, and business franchises have muddied the water on who is responsible for worker safety, leaving the protection of millions of workers uncertain.

State and local government employees also do not receive federal OSHA protections.

A common refrain is that protecting workers is bad for business. But better safety means lower workers’ compensation premiums and fewer claims for business owners. Healthy workers are more productive, less likely to miss work, and more likely to stay with the company. Former Alcoa CEO Paul O’Neill famously made safety the centerpiece of the company’s revitalization.

Alcoa improved upon an already outstanding safety record, created greater operational efficiency, and generated record profits.

Employee-owned companies with Employee Stock Ownership Plans also demonstrate good safety and good business can go hand-in-hand. Research shows they have safer workplaces, less turnover and higher productivity in industries such as manufacturing.

Few jobs have inherent dangers that cannot be mitigated. Most can be designed to be safe. But the fact remains that too many businesses will choose not to protect workers and we need stronger regulations. Workplace inspections are a proven tool. University of Pittsburgh Professor John Mendeloff estimates, for example, that a 60 percent increase in inspections would lead to a 5 percent decrease in fatalities in construction, which would have saved 50 lives in 2020.

But OSHA also needs the capacity to develop standards much more quickly. Stiffer penalties and reforms of the workers compensation system are needed to discourage businesses from being negligent.

AI also holds promise. From flagging high-risk worksites to detecting hazardous exposures, we can choose to deploy technology toward this end. Public-private partnerships that leverage AI to make work safer need to be encouraged if cost is a barrier.

But above all, we need policymakers to prioritize the well-being of their constituents. We need to resource OSHA adequately. An annual budget of $600 million , only a few dollars per worker, is an insult to American workers. The refusal of policymakers to extend federal protections to all workers is simply unconscionable.

Over 100,000 dying per year in any other way would normally catalyze action among policymakers and the public. But if the government’s No. 1 job is to protect Americans, it is sadly failing in the place where most spend a large portion of their days and their lives.

Imagine the productivity and innovation we could unleash if worker health and safety were a priority. More importantly, imagine the millions of family members and friends that would still have their loved ones if workers weren’t treated as disposable. We’ve tackled this problem before. It’s time to finish the work and ensure the workers who make our economy run are not forced to pay for it with their lives and health.

Matt Helmer is director of job quality and worker well-being at the Aspen Institute’s Economic Opportunities Program.

articles.title: Trump promises midterm victory, slams Democrats in Labor Day message
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday promised victory in the upcoming midterm elections for the GOP and went after Democrats in a Labor Day message posted to social media. “Happy Labor Day to all, including the Radical Left Lunatics, Communists, and Dumocrats who will do anything possible to destroy our Country. These Deranged People, after fighting for…
articles.body:
President Trump on Monday promised victory in the upcoming midterm elections for the GOP and went after Democrats in a Labor Day message posted to social media.

“Happy Labor Day to all, including the Radical Left Lunatics, Communists, and Dumocrats who will do anything possible to destroy our Country. These Deranged People, after fighting for 10 years, should finally acknowledge that your Favorite President (ME!), knows how to WIN!” Trump said in a Monday morning post to Truth Social .

“They should be exhausted by now but, sadly, they’re not. They’re going to give it one last shot at ruining America, but we’re not going to let that happen. We’re going to win the Midterms, BIG, and SAVE AMERICA!” he added.

Trump’s post comes amid a challenging time as summer draws to a close. The president’s approval rating is slumping , Democrats have led Republicans in recent polling on the race for Congress, the unpopular war with Iran just passed the six-month mark , and Americans have consistently expressed concerns about the economy .

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ , Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.4 percent as of Monday afternoon, while his disapproval rating was at 57.1 percent.

Last week, Trump urged Republicans in competitive midterm races to run on his record and vowed to campaign alongside them.

The president told GOP lawmakers at a White House dinner that they had successful stories to share with voters in the remaining months of the election season. By telling those stories, the president said they will “win, and you’re going to win big.”

“I’m going to go to every one of those 35 places, and we’re going to see if we can get everyone elected,” the president added, referencing 35 races that will determine the GOP’s hold on the House and the Senate.

Trump is gearing up to speak on both nights of the Republican National Committee’s rare midterm convention slated for later this week.

articles.title: New Mexico Democrats push back over Trump posts about renaming the state ‘New America’
articles.summary: New Mexico Democratic leaders are aggressively pushing back on President Donald Trump’s social media posts about renaming the state of New Mexico as “New America.”
articles.body: New Mexico Democratic leaders are aggressively pushing back on President Donald Trump’s social media posts about renaming the state of New Mexico as “New America.” “New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed,” New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, said in a post on X featuring an image of the state labeled with “New Mexico.” “While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, the price of gas —and everything else — keeps rising. “Under Democratic leadership here in New Mexico, we’re providing families with free childcare and college, protecting access to health care and investing in housing,” the governor continued. “While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work. 🌶️” Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, the Democratic nominee for governor who is vying to succeed Lujan Grisham in November, wrote on X, “I will always stand up for what makes New Mexico, New Mexico” with a video of her at a campaign event. “The only thing I can think of think about when I see that is my opponent, because he’s a Republican, he’s running for New America,” Haaland says in the video. “I’m running to be the governor of New Mexico.” Haaland’s GOP opponent, Gregg Hull, also rejected Trump’s suggestion. “New Mexico does not need a new name,” Hull said in a statement, according to local news outlets. “This state carries the history of Native nations and Spanish explorers who named this land nearly five hundred years ago, and generations of families who built New Mexico into what is is today. That identity is not up for negotiation.” Trump has prompted outrage among New Mexico Democrats and some Republicans when he posted a series of images on Truth Social depicting the state being renamed as “New America.” In an AI-generated post on Sunday, Trump is shown slapping a “New America” over a “Welcome to New Mexico” sign, as he does his signature Trump dance. “Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA,” Trump wrote in the post. “So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!!” On Monday, he continued to post several more images on Truth Social, depicting New Mexico as New America. His latest posts fit a pattern from his presidency, with Trump moving to rename other places on the map. A little more than a week ago, he signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” amid a U.S.-Canada trade war. In January 2025, on his first day back in office, Trump signed an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.” He also renamed Denali, the highest peak in North America, as “Mount McKinley,” after the 25th president. The move infuriated Alaska lawmakers, including those from Trump’s own party. Of course, the president cannot unilaterally change the name of a state the way he can order the federal government to change how it refers to a mountain or a body of water in government databases and documents. The name is spelled out in the opening lines of the state’s constitution: “The name of this state is New Mexico …” To change the name, New Mexico’s voters would need to amend the state constitution. Both of New Mexico’s Democratic senators rejected Trump’s latest posts. “Three things I will always call by their actual names … The Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, New Mexico,” wrote Sen. Martin Heinrich. “It’s New Mexico, always has been and always will be,” added Sen. Ben Ray Lujan. “Just like how you’ll always be a sinvergüenza and corrupt,” he added, using the Spanish word for scoundrel. Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., was perhaps the most blunt of the New Mexico lawmakers: “Oh hell no!” she posted on X. “Our state’s name carries generations of history, culture, and family—and it belongs to us. We’re New Mexicans. Period.”

articles.title: Podcaster apologizes for Lindsay Clancy betting ad
articles.summary: “On Polymarket it was predicted the verdict would be Not Guilty. Are you surprised? #Polymarketpartner,” Hirsch wrote
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The host of a popular podcast has apologized after facing backlash for using the Lindsay Clancy trial in a Polymarket ad on her show.

Amanda Hirsch, host of “Not Skinny But Not Fat,” posted the ad for Polymarket — an online platform that lets users bet on real-life events — the same day the case ended in a mistrial following a hung jury .

“On Polymarket it was predicted the verdict would be Not Guilty. Are you surprised? #Polymarketpartner,” Hirsch wrote. The post has since been deleted.

Ahead of the mistrial, more than $161,000 was wagered on the outcome of Clancy’s trial on Polymarket . The trade wasn’t available to U.S.-based users, only those located outside the country — while it isn’t legal to bet on the outcome of court cases in the U.S. when it comes to standard sportsbooks and federally regulated financial exchanges, prediction sites like Polymarket remain legally ambiguous.

Following backlash, Hirsch called her decision to post about the trial for the brand partnership as “insensitive” and “wrong.”

“I should have known better, and I feel sick that I didn’t see that in the moment,” she wrote in an Instagram post.

Hirsch, a mother herself, says she’s been following the case and “talking about it constantly.” She’d posted previously about the case before the Polymarket ad.

“I became so consumed by the trial that I completely lost perspective and didn’t stop to think about how grossly inappropriate it was to discuss something this tragic in that context,” she wrote.

Clancy’s trial has captured national attention and sparked highly emotional debates over mental health, as well as conspiracy theories surrounding the case.

articles.title: Thousands protest against AfD in Berlin after election victory
articles.summary: Several thousand people gathered at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on Monday evening to protest against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) following its...
articles.body:
Several thousand people gathered at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on Monday evening to protest against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) following its landslide victory in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

Police estimated the crowd at around 5,000 and said the demonstration passed without incident.

Among those taking part were prominent German climate activist Luisa Neubauer and the lead candidates of the Greens and The Left in Berlin's state election on September 20.

Protesters carried banners with slogans including "Fascism is not an alternative" and "Stop AfD Nazis! End racism and social cuts," while crowds chanted: "All together against fascism!"

The party won Sunday's election by a wide margin but fell short of an absolute majority, leaving open the possibility of Germany's first AfD-led state government.

The domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD's state branch as "confirmed right-wing extremist."

Hundreds of people also gathered in nearby Potsdam on Monday evening to protest against the AfD.
